articles.fullContent: The European Commission went from a Matrix proof of concept in December 2025 to a sovereign communication tool rolled out to every Commission laptop by September 2026. That tool, built on Matrix by Element ,and run by the Commission itself, now serves more than 40,000 users.At Matrix Conference 2026, Diana Gheorghe, Head of Sector for Digital Workplace Communication and Collaboration Services, and Alexandru Vignide, Service Delivery Manager for the Commission's sovereign communication tool, told the story of how they got there. The pair were transparent about what got harder at scale, and how they dealt with it. Sovereignty means more than where the servers sit“Sovereignty” can have a different meaning for different people and organisations, so the Commission started by pinning down what it means for them. Their answer spans five dimensions: resilience and business continuity, vendor diversity, control over their data, ownership of the platform, and leverage in procurement - the ability to negotiate with, or walk away from, a supplier. That last one is easy to forget, and arguably the one that bites hardest when it's missing.For internal communications specifically, the priorities were resilience, data ownership and, crucially, interoperability. That's what led them to Matrix: an open protocol whose value lies in letting separate systems talk to each other. They chose Element Server Suite Pro (ESS Pro), Element's enterprise distribution of Matrix, as a mature implementation, and decided to host, operate and architect the service under their own control.Sovereign cloud hosting, familiar login, without federation (yet)With the building blocks chosen, Alexandru walked through three architecture decisions.Hosting. The service doesn't run in a Commission-owned data centre. Instead it runs with sovereign cloud providers selected through the sovereign hosting tender awarded earlier this year, in order to meet its sovereignty and hosting requirements. Sovereign doesn't have to mean building everything in-house; it means choosing who you depend on, and on what terms.Identity. The deployment is integrated with EU Login, the sign-in staff already use every day. A new tool is easier to adopt when logging in feels familiar.Federation. Connecting to Matrix servers outside the Commission is still under assessment. The technical side is being explored - there was a separate hands-on demo using non-production environments at the conference - but federation also needs governance, participation and structure, which takes longer to agree than a config change.Nine months from proof of concept to every Commission laptopThe Commission started working with Matrix in summer 2025, or, as Alexandru put it, at last year's Matrix Conference. From there, things moved quickly:December 2025: the architecture and engineering team delivered a proof of concept showing Matrix and Element were viable for the Commission. It earned a green light for a Commission-wide service, which Alexandru described as a nice Christmas present.January to June 2026: the team built the production infrastructure, along with the hosting and operations needed to run it, and was ready by June.Pilots: a laptop pilot covering both the desktop and web clients, followed by a mobile pilot through the Commission's mobile device management (MDM) platform.July to September 2026: the laptop rollout to all Commission users, delivered in waves, was and completed in September.The Commission is now exploring a mobile rollout, and what federation could look like.Scaling to 40,000 users brought challengesRolling out to 40,000 people surfaces problems no pilot will. Alexandru described the four main ones his team ran into, and how they tackled each.Finding colleagues across servers. articles.fullContent: AI has changed a lot. We do more work in parallel. This increases the memory demand on our workstations. Also, memory is expensive and often not extendable. So buying more RAM is not an easy option. Recently I was running out of memory, I found my solution in zram, a solution to compress memory.Memory compression is not new. If you have a Windows or Mac device you are already using it. Also, many Android smartphones utilize the technique of using compression to put more data into the RAM. Unfortunately not all Linux environments have RAM compression enabled by default. Fedora, Pop!_OS do, but Ubuntu doesn’t. Amazon Linux only enables zram on smaller virtual machines. Most other distributions do not have it enabled.Compressing memory does come with small, but not really noticeable, downsides. It takes a little bit more from your CPU and adds latency to some processes. What you gain is gigantic amounts of extra capacity. It is not uncommon to see compression ratios up to 1:4.I remember that in the early days of writing SaaS software we would often need double the size of the machines when we added more features to our monolithic app. Often the CPUs were under little stress, so we could have avoided upgrading if we had enabled RAM compression. articles.fullContent: TLDR; We built Blobasaur, a sharded, distributed, lightweight blob storage server on top of SQLite to solve our high-throughput blob read/write usecase. JSON blobs varying from a few KBs to MBs are now written and read thousands of times per second on commodity hardware while maintaining single-digit millisecond latency.On Kite, our trading platform with ~20 million customers, users are able to customize their investment and trading screens heavily. They save multi-chart layouts, financial indicator templates, vector drawings, and various kinds of arbitrary UI preferences. In addition, we offer a Terminal mode that allows users to design their own workspaces by dragging, dropping, and customizing widgets. Under the hood, our backend services store these user preferences and metadata as opaque blobs (mostly JSON) ranging from a few kilobytes to several megabytes.Many years ago, we stored such blobs in CouchDB, which turned out to be ill-suited for the kind of throughput we were starting to see. We then moved to SSDB (ssdb), a C++ disk-backed store that speaks the Redis protocol. This made it very easy to integrate as well. SSDB solved our immediate performance problems and ran reliably in production for several years.Over time, two problems forced us to look for a replacement:SSDB became unmaintained, which was an obvious operational risk. It is written in C++, which is not a part of our stack or expertise, so forking and maintaining was also not viable.Scaling and size limits. SSDB is not a distributed system and can only run on a single node. This imposes significant future scaling challenges, including at one point forcing us to cap blob sizes at 1 MB because latency degrades on larger payloads.As we added features like the Terminal mode and onboarded more internal services, we needed a robust solution. Our criteria were:A key-value blob store with a simple API.Designed for multi-megabyte blob read/write ops and high throughput. We sustain loads of thousands to tens of thousands of requests per second reading and writing arbitrary blobs. These are unpredictable and bursty thanks to the volatility in stock markets.Horizontally scalable, distributed.Disk-space efficiency / compression.Easily maintainable and highly economical.So we investigated FOSS databases optimized for high-throughput blob storage and looked at the following:ScyllaDB: We already run ScyllaDB for high-throughput workloads, but in our tests, it turned out to be suboptimal for large blobs. Significantly lower throughput and higher resource usage. We specifically want multi-megabyte blobs. Tombstones from frequent overwrites and TTL expiries require careful tuning in ScyllaDB.PostgreSQL: We already have considerable experience with Postgres in our stack and experimented with storing blobs as BYTEA columns, but it turned out to be severely suboptimal again for the use case in terms of performance and disk-space efficiency.YugabyteDB: Has blob storage as one of the options, but is not primarily designed or optimized for it. Also, a large system with too many features.RocksDB: Had the right primitives, but again, not architected for high throughput multi-MB blob writes.Ceph: Severe operational complexity and resource requirements. We didn’t even get to trying it out.SeaweedFS: This was the closest candidate. However, there were a few blockers. Our use case is overwrite-heavy (a user changing their workspace) over the same key, and SeaweedFS keeps appending before compaction, which can cause disk usage to grow uncontrollably. Blobs have their own IDs, which then have to be mapped against user keys in a separate DB, adding another layer. It doesn’t support TTL per blob. Also, reasonably complex setup with many parts.S3 and MinIO: Object storage has high per-request latency for small blobs, high request costs under write-heavy workloads (writes are 50% of our traffic), and coarse lifecycle TTLs instead of exact key expiry. Nov 18, 2026Put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, big demand - there aren’t enough web servers for everyone. Let’s run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them. I couldn’t get funding, so we’re bootstrapping. The goal is to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 10GB of RAM and 1 CPU core. If we succeed, I’ll find some RAM from old microwaves around the house and we’ll scale it up so everyone can have their own web server. Demand will drop to zero and cybersecurity will be solved once and for all.Web serverInstead of vibe coding it all, let’s use an ancient technique called learning. First of all, what is a web server? There are a few essential syscalls.listen - syscall, asks kernel to listen for connections on a socketaccept - syscall, accepts a connection on a socketrecv - receives data from a socketsend - sends dataclose - closesWhat is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Let’s use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with OK.int main(void) { // We use port 0 which makes OS return any available port int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); if (listen(server, 128) < 0) return 1; const char reply[] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Content-Length: 2

OK"; for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); } }It couldn’t be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that we’ve learned everything, let’s finish the article and call it a day:$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server &; done ... ... 28232 program exited with error 1Hm, why did listen fail? Ah, we’ve run out of ports! We’re using port=0, so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range.$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768 60999Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/).Ports 1-1024 require root.Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You don’t want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535, but that’s still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Technical details Root cause Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital ß. Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS, but the loop only bounds-checks one (to < to_end). while (*pp < end && to < to_end) { /* room for one byte */ code = *(*pp)++; if (code == SHARP_s) { if (flags & ONIGENC_CASE_UPCASE) { *to++ = 'S'; /* first byte */ code = 'S'; } /* ... */ } /* ... */ *to++ = code; /* second byte, unchecked */} The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20 bytes. Each ß adds one byte to the output, so an input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte. The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?. UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected. Fixed upstream in ruby/ruby@d582f8f. Primitive A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S (0x53) when upcasing or s (0x73) when case-folding, and it lands directly after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the buffer through the input length. Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of bounds. articles.fullContent: Posted by mame on 18 Nov 2026 Seven vulnerabilities have been discovered in Ruby’s regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution. We have released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 to fix them. We strongly recommend upgrading. CVE identifiers have been requested for these vulnerabilities but have not been assigned yet, so this advisory refers to them by their GitHub Security Advisory (GHSA) identifiers. GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5: Heap buffer overflow in case conversion of strings Ruby has a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x: Double free in regular expression compilation Ruby has a double free in its regular expression engine. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px: Integer overflow in case conversion of strings Ruby has an integer overflow in the case conversion of strings, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r: Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive regular expression matching Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching against a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that use attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can lead to memory corruption in an attacker-controlled way. GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w: Heap buffer overflow in regular expression compilation Ruby has an integer overflow in its regular expression engine, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-7whj-cfh7-xgm4: Heap buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s Ruby has a heap-based buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s. Converting a crafted regular expression to a string may allow information disclosure or remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h: Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive backreference matching Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching a crafted string may disclose memory contents or crash the process. Affected versions Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier Ruby 3.4.0 through 3.4.12 Ruby 4.0.0 through 4.0.9 Recommended action We strongly recommend upgrading to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14. Ruby 3.3 is in the security maintenance phase. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached their end of life and will not receive these fixes. articles.fullContent: I have been hacking both hardware and software for 2 decades. Previously manually. But in 2026 with the help of AIs the proccess is greatly sped up. Below I will describe my proccess briefly or how I do it. Set Up Tools which I mostly use are these: Process What I basically do nowadays is just point the agent at the binary to be analysed and use my set of dedicated agent skills. Rest usually takes care of itself. But putting the skills besides, the flow is basically this. Find binary type, platform, build etc - based on this using appropriate decompiler (note - current AIs do fairly well with just disassembly . ie pure x86 or ARM instructions). Command agent to document all findings along the way to MD files. This serves several purposes. They become notes for your own understanding. They help the agent not lose the track after compaction / handoff to different agent. And last but not least, it helps the agent work more effectively, not get lost in circles etc. More about this later. Ask the agent to analyse basic structure. Main functions, main branching, imported functions etc of given binary. By binary I mean whatever. Desktop executable, website or firmware image. Once I have this basic overview I can usually proceed any way I need to do modifications to the original binary or build mods or just help me understand it better. On some occasions some things are not easily resolvable by simple disassembly or decompilation. In those cases you can do: Let the agent debug given binary and set breakpoints on specific parts to help it figure out given inner workings. Use logging. Either by somehow enabling it in the original binary or by making a probe (and this can mean many things) that injects to the original binary and records you via logs (to file) whatever is needed to resolve given feature. Give agent outside access - ie computer use for desktop apps, or api controllable emulator for running and controlling given firmware. Ask agent to try different approach. But you must be specific. Ie when it gets stuck in disasembly by following xrefs, ask it to try to follow strings in the binary instead. Read the entire LLM conversation and thinking. Current LLMs are smart but they still sometimes get to a narrow approach. By reading the traces you can often instinctively figure the agent it going into a blind path and give it suggestion as to how it might be approached better. That however skill of your own to have. SKILLS Here are some of my major skills I use frequently. Matt Pottock - Grill me It gives you several questions when your input might be valuable. I usually use it with this prompt: text Use skill /grill-me to ask me up to 5 questions whose answers are crucial for your further progress. Ask only one question at a time. mattpocockskillsShellSkills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory.Open repo Opens in a new tab. Ghidra / other RE tooling skill It helps a ton to have a skill where your specific reverse engineering tooling is described. Ie to use radare2 or kuna. Or description of how to use the MCP Ghidra bridge and for what. Without such a skill, agents often give up too quickly getting lost, not knowing how to do the actual disassembly / decompilation. ioma8ghidra-decompile-skillJavaAgent skill + 22 Ghidra scripts for fast targeted decompilation, and the fix for GhidraMCP extension/Ghidra version mismatches.Open repo Opens in a new tab. Hypothesis debugging That is also my own skill. Its related to how I wrote earlier how important it is to make the agent document everything into MD files. This skill forces agent who is getting stuck to follow this loop: Make a hypothesis of why / how something works. Write it down into CSV table of hypotheses, saved on disc. Design experiment (probe, logging, ...) which will definitively prove or disprove this hypothesis. Record the result. Repeat. This is variation of scientific method and it significantly helps agents when they are getting stuck on some problem. Stop

articles.fullContent: Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.We are releasing BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints for everyone to try and build on. In this post, we explain how carefully designed tasks and efficient infrastructure made these gains possible on a limited compute budget.DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above1. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, a notoriously hard long-horizon benchmark. Our magic lies in the following three key ingredients: high-quality training data, efficient training backend, and robust sandboxes.High-quality Training DataWe built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from Eigent AI’s large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 of them made it into the final training set. The training tasks are selected based on three criteria.Each task targets a mistake the original model makes. We ran the original Qwen3.8-27B on every training task and carefully redesigned each one so that it brings out the mistakes we want the model to stop making. We then tuned each task until its solve rate fell within a suitable range, neither too easy nor too hard for the model to learn from.Every task is a long job with several problems chained together. Each task entails a chain of interdependent problems, so an agent has to navigate through multiple stages of reasoning, planning, and execution. Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in the sandbox, with more than 100 tool-calls and more than 256k output tokens.There is no room for reward hacking. We reviewed every task along with the model's attempts at it. Any task that could be passed without really solving it, or that had a design flaw, was fixed or removed before training.Efficient training backendRadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. articles.fullContent: Vertigo is a massively parallel RISC-V emulator running on Nvidia GPU hardware, that boots one Linux kernel image with a BusyBox uClibc userspace, and runs it on thousands of emulated CPU cores simultaneously, sharing a single address space, cooperating through the same kernel, and using the same scheduler. Each core/hart has its own register file and hardware thread state, the memory they address is one flat space held in VRAM. The result is one Linux machine with thousands of processors, running entirely on GPU hardware. The Problem A symmetric multiprocessor is expensive to study. Scaling experiments require either access to real hardware with many cores, which is scarce, or simulation, which is slow. Existing simulators that model SMP behaviour run at a fraction of the speed of the target and typically model a handful of cores. Studying scheduler behaviour, lock contention, cache effects, and NUMA topology at scale requires either access to real hardware or a fast enough simulator. A modern GPU has tens of thousands of hardware execution units and high-bandwidth memory, so in my opinion that makes it a natural fit for a simulation that needs many cores sharing one address space. The obstacle is that GPU threads are designed for data-parallel workloads, not branchy interpretation, so a single GPU thread is slower than a CPU core at interpretation. The real question is whether thousands of GPU threads together can simulate a large SMP machine fast enough to be practical. The Relationship to Chimera Chimera multiplies one Linux image across many isolated namespaces. Each namespace believes it owns the machine, so none of them can reach any other. The isolation is structural: separate register files, separate private memory slices, one shared read-only kernel image. Chimera's design problem is isolation with minimal per-namespace cost. Vertigo inverts the model. There is one machine, the CPUs share everything: one physical address space, kernel, scheduler, set of page tables. The design problem is coherence rather than isolation. Where Chimera works hard to prevent one namespace from observing another, Vertigo works hard to make all cores observe the same state in the right order. The emulator substrate is almost the same. The memory access path, fetch-decode-execute loop, CSR emulation, CLINT, UART, and the bounded execution model are all inherited from Chimera. The additions are: coherence protocol, inter-processor interrupt mechanism, PLIC, and SMP-capable hardware surface that Linux requires. Memory Layout VRAM holds one flat guest address space shared by all cores. guest physical: [ 0x80000000 kernel, initramfs, device tree, heap, stacks RAM_SIZE bytes ] VRAM: [ RAM one copy, RAM_SIZE bytes, read and write by all cores ] [ cpu_t array one entry per core, register file and CSR set ] [ pending_ipi one word per core, the incoming IPI bitmask ] There are no private slices, a write by core N to address A is visible to core M when core M reads address A. This is the contract a symmetric multiprocessor makes with its software, and it is the contract the Linux SMP kernel requires. Vertigo honours it by making every store go to global memory and every load come from global memory. The GPU's own memory model is weaker than that, so enforcing the contract requires explicit fence instructions in the emulator where the guest issues fence instructions. The RAM template is uploaded once before the kernel launches, all cores start from the same image. Core 0 runs the kernel boot path, cores 1 through N-1 spin on a secondary entry address, waiting for core 0 to release them through the SMP boot protocol. Emulated Hardware Vertigo emulates a minimal RV64GC machine sufficient to boot an SMP NOMMU or MMU Linux kernel, so the emulated hardware surface is larger than Chimera's because SMP Linux requires more of it. articles.fullContent: What it is A QR code looks like noise, but every square has a job. A few help a camera find the code and line it up. A few say how the rest is encoded. In this one the text itself fills only about a quarter of the squares, and almost half are spare data that can rebuild parts that get damaged. QR Anatomy builds one code from scratch, labels every square, and lets you damage it to watch the repairs work. What you can do Point at any square. The Inspector names it: a corner finder, a timing mark, format bit 12, or one bit of the spare data. All 8 squares of that byte light up. Scratch it. Click, drag, or press Scratch 10. The page re-reads the code after every change and shows each block filling its repair budget, until one overflows and the code dies. See how it was built. The bits of the message, the blocks of bytes, the zigzag path they’re laid along, all eight masks with their scores, and the 15 format bits. Checked against a real decoder The encoder is about 1,250 lines of Python with no dependencies. To make sure its codes are real ones, the tests have an independent decoder, zxing-cpp, read all 160 combinations of size (versions 1 to 40) and error-correction level, with all 8 masks. Another test checks that the page’s JavaScript decoder agrees with the Python one. The repair is Reed-Solomon, the classic machinery: Berlekamp-Massey finds where the errors are, with Chien search and Forney’s formula working out the fixes. Honest limits The decoder starts from a clean grid of squares. It doesn’t find a code in a photo, so scratches on the corner finders, timing marks and alignment pattern don’t hurt it. Scratches on the format bits do. The encoder runs in Python, not in the page, so this shows one code and you can’t type your own text. articles.fullContent: I’ve long enjoyed taking part in CTF competitions and solving machines on Hack The Box and TryHackMe, so I need a lot of tools installed on my system to tackle all these challenges. I didn’t want to clutter my system with a bunch of utilities and one-off scripts that, by the way, you can’t always trust either, so here’s how I solved that problem.How I ended up using a containerThe obvious and simplest solution was to use my main operating system. But I didn’t like that approach from the very first day I got interested in CTFs, because you can’t always fully check exploit scripts downloaded from the internet. From a security standpoint, that’s no good at all.So I initially used a separate operating system running in a virtual machine. At different points, I used different distributions: Kali Linux, Parrot OS, BlackArch. It worked: all the basic tools were there, I could install more, a virtual machine is an isolated environment, and I could also share files from the host by mounting a host directory in the guest. I used this approach for many years, but it had plenty of drawbacks I always had to put up with. Overall, these were the pros and cons:ProsConsThe system runs in an isolated environment without access to the host filesystem, which is great when security is a concern.Besides your main system, you also have to configure and update the guest. I agree that ideally you shouldn’t bother with this, but still, once you get used to certain keyboard shortcuts and tools, you want to use them in the virtual environment too.You can move the virtual machine image to another computer and keep using it without any trouble. I had to do this at least a couple of times.The guest system is slower than the host, so you have to spend time on optimization and configuration.Convenient access to files from the host. You can even mount specific directories read-only.A guest system with lots of tools starts taking up a huge amount of space over time, essentially turning into a dumping ground. Thankfully, it’s not your main system, but you still have to think about it and find compromises.Before running an unverified exploit or experimenting with settings, you can save the system state and restore it in a couple of seconds if needed.A virtual machine takes time to start. Annoying, but still something you can live with.That was how I approached CTFs for a long time. After that, I decided to install a second operating system alongside my main one and switch between them. This meant rebooting the computer, but working in a full environment is still nicer than working in a virtual one. Living with two systems, I quickly realized this wasn’t for me, because it came with almost all the drawbacks of a virtual machine, plus the constant rebooting. So I soon arrived at my current setup: a Docker container.More about the Docker imageOf course, I started by looking at my options, meaning which existing Docker images I could use. Kali Linux provides an official image, but as an Arch Linux fan and devotee, I soon started looking at the BlackArch Linux image. The BlackArch Linux base image is maintained and updated, and that’s what I decided to build on. What it lacked were frequently used tools and some configuration I needed, like an advanced shell and a nice-looking Vim setup, but the main thing was that the packages I use regularly weren’t preinstalled. Docker lets you take an image as a base and build your own on top of it, which is exactly what I did.An interesting detail about the BlackArch Linux Docker image is that there are actually two images: one for terminal use and another for GUI use through noVNC . I decided to use the second one as my base so I could run graphical applications, and accepted the larger image size as a trade-off, since I knew my image would be large anyway: I was going to preinstall all the tools I needed.The image is updated, built, and published to Docker Hub every day through GitHub Actions.How I use the BlackArch Docker cont

It is a static analysis pass that must provably terminate and provably uphold four invariants per instruction: C1 — DAG termination: No unbounded loops. Enforced via CFG back-edge detection; the only sanctioned cycle is bpf_loop() (kernel ≥ 5.17) with a runtime callback whose iteration count is bounded at verification time. Legacy bounded loops (kernel ≥ 5.3) are unrolled — a loop with MAYBE-wide trip count N expands the explored state space by N. C2 — Instruction budget: BPF_COMPLEXITY_LIMIT_INSNS = 1,000,000 (6.x; 128k hard cap pre-5.2 with BPF_MAXINSNS = 4096 per program for non-privileged). The verifier explores paths, not instructions — worst case state explosion is O(branches^depth), and a 4k-instruction program with data-dependent branches can exhaust 1M processed instructions in ~60ms on a Zen 3. C3 — Register state soundness: Every register carries a struct bpf_reg_state with a type (SCALAR_VALUE, PTR_TO_MAP_VALUE, PTR_TO_BTF_ID, PTR_TO_STACK, …), a tnum (tracked-numbers abstraction: mask|value bitpair encoding), and 32/64-bit ranges. Precision analysis (kernel ≥ 5.4) does back-propagation to prune imprecise branches that would otherwise fork the state tree. C4 — Memory safety: Every load/store must resolve to a statically known region with bounds proven by the tnum/range lattice. The response (●) makes the same trip in reverse. The Wi-Fi radio is never touched. § 01 The short answer localhost, in one paragraph Quick answerlocalhost is the standard hostname for the computer you're using right now. Your operating system maps it to a special loopback address — 127.0.0.1 in IPv4, ::1 in IPv6 — so anything sent there turns around inside your machine instead of going out to the network. Zoom 010 mYour computer When you open http://localhost:3000, your browser and your server are two programs on the same machine. The request goes down your operating system's network stack, reaches the loopback interface — a network card made entirely of software — and comes straight back up to the program listening on port 3000. No Wi-Fi, no router, no internet. That's why localhost is fast, private, and works on a plane. articles.fullContent: Describe a small 3D scene as JSON and get a flat SVG picture of it from any angle. Inspired by Zdog. Pronounced "zee-pup". These four pictures come from one scene: eleven solids with one color each, plus a door and a window, placed in 3D. Only the view angle differs. Zpup works out what hides what and how each face is shaded, and writes a plain SVG with no JavaScript, so the picture works in an tag, an email or a README. One view of the lighthouse is 5.5 KB. Try it in the playground: edit a scene as JSON, drag the picture to turn it, and export the SVG. Compared with Zdog Both halves are the same solids at the same places and sizes (Zdog script, Zpup scene); the Zdog half is a flip-book of Zdog's own SVG output, one frame every 3 degrees. Watch the hut and the boulder as they pass behind the tower: in Zdog the island is painted over them. Zdog orders shapes by one point each, so a large shape such as the ground covers smaller ones that sit on it once they are farther away than its center. In Zdog the fix is done by hand, with groups or by cutting the large shape up. Zpup compares every pair of shapes that overlap on screen and works out which one is in front. In the benchmark, the median share of a picture painted in the wrong order was 2.9% and 4.2% for Zdog in two runs, and 0.4% and 0.3% for Zpup. What it is for Small illustrations with volume: icons, mascots, props, a little building. The scene is data, so a person, a script or an AI model can write it, and mistakes come back as errors that say where and how to fix them. Each picture links to its scene, 60 to 150 lines of TypeScript. The cactus uses soft shading. It is not a 3D engine. There is no perspective, no textures and no light to place, and shapes that cut deep into each other are not drawn correctly. There is no text shape and no clipping either. For that, use three.js or a modeling tool. Status Early, and the API may still change before 1.0. The one animation available is a constant turn about one axis (see Turning in place). Install Zpup is ESM-only and has no runtime dependencies. It is built for ES2022 and tested on Node 24; it uses no Node APIs, so it also runs in browsers. Bundled and minified, the whole library is 69 KB (26 KB gzipped), and renderSvg alone is 50 KB (19 KB gzipped). articles.contentSnippet: I have started using multiple models (Claude, Codex, Grok via cursor-agent, Z.ai, Deepseek, Hy4 via OpenCode, agy) etc, and I realized that I not able to identify which commit was made by which model.   After looking around and not finding anything, I create a  format specification that will let Model self-identify itself. The goal is a higher ranked model can verify the output of other models and suggest changes. It is similar how to a Senior Engineer will review the output of Junior Engineers.
articles.fullContent: Model Identification hook for Git Commits It is desirable to have model and model properties identification in git commits authored by AI models. This repository provides a git hook that enforces a commit message format and a review workflow. Every AI-authored commit carries a one-line self-identification, so a stronger model can review it later and know who wrote it and how sure they were. A git hook can't instruct a model directly, so commit-msg rejects the commit with instructions. The agent reads the error, adds the trailers, and retries. It works with any agent that runs git commit. What a commit looks like Add retry backoff to fetch Model: claude-sonnet-5-5 harness=claude-code effort=high conf=medium Full format and rules: SPEC.md. Install cd your-repo && /path/to/install.sh # this repo only (core.hooksPath -> this project's hooks/) /path/to/install.sh --global # all repos (copies hooks to ~/.config/git/hooks) Global install copies the hooks, so re-run it after updating them. It also overrides any per-repo .git/hooks. Use Agents: commit normally; if rejected, follow the printed instructions. Humans: GIT_HUMAN_COMMIT=1 git commit ... skips the check. Merges, reverts are exempt automatically Review workflow post-commit copies the Model trailer into git notes --ref=model-id with Review-Status: pending. bin/model-review list [range] # self-ID + status per commit bin/model-review comment <sha> "<text>" # reviewer comment -> refs/notes/model-review; marks reviewed git push origin refs/notes/model-id refs/notes/model-review # notes are not pushed by default The trailer in the commit message is the source of truth; notes are an index and can be lost on amend/rebase. Limits The identification is self-reported: a model can misstate its own ID or confidence if it is instructed to do so. License Apache License 2.0 - see LICENSE for details. articles.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explains why he asked 60K employees to quit
articles.contentSnippet: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit, rather than reducing the workforce via another massive layoff. The short answer is AI, but not in the way you might expect.
articles.fullContent: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff. Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect. He’s not saying he’s replacing employees with AI, especially software engineers. He’s saying he’s reorganizing Microsoft into a company where everyone uses AI to do their work, and their jobs become focused on managing that AI. The buyout was “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices,” he told Andrew Ross Sorkin during the DealBook Summit. “Let’s take software engineering. We went from, ‘Well, we don’t buy that AI can ever do software.’ To suddenly, ‘Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?’ To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point,” he explained. For some people, “that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?” he added, “but, I mean, it has to be done.” He offered the example of the team that builds Cowork, the AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps. He said the team consists of just 11 developers who have mastered using AI to do their jobs. “They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product.” He believes that every employee will one day similarly become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work. “That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs.” But Microsoft, as a 51-year-old company, didn’t grow up as an AI-first company. “So the question is, how quickly can an incumbent transform the work, the workflow, and the work artifact, and with all the wage support that goes with it?” he said. “It’s going to take a bit more time than anyone expects. And there is going to be in all of this, you know, people who may say, ‘Hey, I have some other choices I want to make.’” When asked about this same topic — why ask 60,000 people to voluntarily resign — last week by Gergely Orosz on his The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Nadella further explained, “We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don’t have control of their own destiny because the way we have talked about this AI revolution.” He called out talk about the singularity (the hypothetical point at which AI surpasses human intelligence) and predictions that AI will take away all jobs. “All of that leads anyone who even wants to change to be sort of anxious … You have to sort of walk the hard walk of really making the structural changes, getting people slotted, giving them opportunity.” In other words, the buyout was the message to employees: You can get with the new AI-first program, which will radically change your job, or you choose to get on with your life. articles.title: Elon Musk says: ‘I’m not MAGA’
articles.contentSnippet: During his appearance Wednesday at The New York Times' DealBook Summit, Elon Musk said that he wasn't sure what the term "MAGA" meant and also commented that he felt "pretty foolish" for having spent so much money during the U.S. midterms.
articles.fullContent: Elon Musk, who spent $277 million to get Donald Trump reelected president in 2024 and who, during that campaign, declared himself “dark MAGA” and who, after the election, was subsequently photographed sporting a cartoonishly large MAGA hat while visiting the Oval Office, has some news for Americans: None of that necessarily makes him MAGA. “I’m not MAGA,” Musk declared Wednesday during a conversation with Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times DealBook Summit. Musk joined the conversation via video call, as he is currently in China, joining President Trump for the APEC summit. “Well, at least I’m not like … I’m not sure what MAGA means,” he backtracked. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.” The comments were made amidst a broader question about how Musk felt in the wake of this year’s midterms, during which a “blue wave” led to Democratic victories throughout the country. Musk, notably, spent a gargantuan amount of money (reportedly some $445 million) to support Republican candidates. Musk admitted Wednesday that such vast political spending might not have been a good use of his money. “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seen much for it,” he said. “Or maybe it would have been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that, you know, American elections are not just about money.” During his conversation with Sorkin, Musk also seemed to lean away from his viral edgelord persona and claimed that he held no extreme views. He said: “I don’t think I have like, you know, any kind of extreme political views.” Sorkin pushed Musk on this a little, noting that some people found his views on immigration extreme, to which Musk said: “Like what?” Mild laughter spread throughout the audience. Ironically, the last time Musk spoke at DealBook, in 2023, he was in the middle of a very public battle with his social media site X’s advertisers. Critics had accused Musk of platforming a typhoon of hateful content on his site, and advertisers were threatening to walk over it. In response, Musk famously told Sorkin that he hoped those advertisers would “go f—” themselves. Now Musk has an entirely new set of concerns. Democratic lawmakers in various committees have signaled that they may investigate Musk and his business activities as they probe potential corruption throughout the Trump administration. Specifically, officials have said they’re interested in scrutinizing Musk’s role in DOGE, the “government efficiency” initiative that Musk launched inside the White House at the start of Trump’s new term, as well as Starlink’s activities in Ukraine, where the company has been accused of throttling the military’s access to its internet service. Sorkin broached some of the potential concerns for the Tesla CEO: “You hear people like the chairman of the oversight committee saying, ‘Lawyer up,’ and you hear the president saying, ‘If I have to give him a pardon’ — meaning you — ‘I’ll give him a pardon.’” Musk replied: “I don’t think I need a pardon by the way, because I haven’t committed any crimes.” Musk then made one of those controversial statements he’s known for, appearing to compare an incoming Texas official to Lavrentiy Beria, the top head of the Soviet secret police under Josef Stalin. “The incoming Texas, you know, House Majority Leader, said that I should go to prison,” Musk said. “I’m like, the guy’s trying to, you know channel Beria from, like, Stalin, where it’s, you know, show me the man, I’ll show you the crime type of thing.” It’s not clear who (or what) Musk was talking about. Texas doesn’t have a House Majority Leader. However, he may have been referencing Gene Wu, who is the incoming chair of the Texas House Democratic caucus and who has suggested that Musk be investigated for potential criminal activity. “Hopefully, in this country, you still need to do an actual crime before you go to prison,” Musk added. articles.title: Amidst fears of AI cyberattacks, Satya Nadella says lots of critical infrastructure is ‘unpatchable’
articles.contentSnippet: The Microsoft CEO downplayed the recent Outlook outage while noting that AI was causing both opportunities and new challenges for securing much of the connected world.
articles.fullContent: During his appearance at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella lamented the fact that a lot of America’s software systems — including those governing everyday hardware and transportation systems — suffer from unfixable software vulnerabilities that, in the age of AI-aided cyberattacks, are just waiting to be exploited. “Remember, there is a lot of stuff in our critical infrastructure that’s unpatchable,” Nadella said. “I mean, think about all the firmware and the chillers [a cooling device often used in data centers] and the HVAC systems everywhere else. So all of that, by the way, they’re on the internet.” In other words: The smartification of the economy, in which much of the world’s “dumb” devices were hooked up to the internet, is now causing tremendous headaches. The conversation took place against the backdrop of a wave of recent large-scale outages — including one involving Microsoft Outlook. Others have involved the NSA, the FFA, and Apple. Concerns have swirled that these outages are the result of cyberattacks, although officials have denied those claims. Still, the reality of AI-aided cyberattacks is spurring companies to find new strategies for vulnerability discovery and remediation. Nadella touched briefly on the recent Outlook situation, noting that the global inconvenience was the result of a “latent bug” that led to a “perfect storm.” “We put out an incident response, and we’re going to obviously take all of the learnings, both upstream architectural, as well as operational, and fix that,” he added. “Somebody was telling me about sort of even the transportation systems and the amount of stuff that’s discoverable but with unpatchable firmware,” Nadella also added on the topic of vulnerable systems. “So we’ll have to really modernize for sure … and then we will have to assess what the threat vector looks like, what our own ability to both detect and then defend in real time looks like.” Nadella made a broader point as well, which is that the process of patching software vulnerabilities has escalated to match the speed of potential exploitation, but that this has caused more problems. “We now have a very powerful tool that finds vulnerabilities,” he said. However, companies used to have more time to test those patches, understand a situation, and deploy them, he said. At the same time, AI has made sophisticated cyberattacks much easier to enact. “The patch [now] needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production, because it’s being exploited in the wild, right? So that’s going to create instability.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. articles.title: Elon Musk says ousting Jensen Huang is like ‘kicking Michael Jordan off your team’
articles.contentSnippet: “I don’t think [Huang is] disloyal to the United States," Musk said.
articles.fullContent: Elon Musk has already been vocal about his disapproval of the Nvidia board’s decision to oust its founder and CEO Jensen Huang after a series of extramarital affairs were made public, including one with an alleged Chinese spy who is suspected of feeding sensitive information back to Beijing. At The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Musk elaborated on his thoughts about Nvidia’s leadership change. “Jensen is an old friend of mine,” Musk said. “I would call Jensen, you know, Michael Jordan at his peak level, in terms of what he means to a team.” On X, the social media platform he owns, Musk even said he would hire Huang. “He’s one of the most talented entrepreneur-CEOs in history,” Musk said when asked about his X post. “Who wouldn’t want to hire Jensen?” Musk also signed a petition, alongside over 200,000 other people, urging Nvidia to reinstate its former CEO. Nvidia’s board, however, confirmed it is not planning to bring Huang back. “[It] doesn’t seem like a smart decision to me…” Musk said of that decision. “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen.” Huang “has long-term relationships that have been built up over decades,” Musk added. “He understands technology incredibly well. His team loves him… and many of them are there because of him, and have higher offers to go elsewhere, and have turned them down because of personal loyalty to Jensen.” Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey also said that he thinks Nvidia is making the wrong decision by not reinstating Huang. “China wants Jensen out, so I want him in,” Luckey said earlier in the day at the DealBook event. “They’re thrilled to have Jensen out… There’s a reason it’s knocking a trillion dollars off Nvidia’s market cap. They know it makes America weaker to knock him out.” Musk also did not express concern over what Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy could mean for U.S. national security. “I don’t think he’s disloyal to the United States,” Musk said. “I think it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak, and it just doesn’t seem like a good thing for shareholders.” Other peers in the industry, like Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, reaffirmed their faith in Nvidia to move forward without its founder and CEO of 33 years at the helm. “It’s the Nvidia board’s decision, but I’ll just say this one thing,” Nadella said at DealBook. “Colette [Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia] worked at Microsoft for a long time. I’ve known her for a long time. She’s a tremendous person… I have a lot of confidence in the Nvidia team and their ability to continue to do the good work.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella remains confident in Nvidia after Huang’s exit
articles.contentSnippet: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella expressed confidence in Jensen Huang's successor Colette Kress, who is serving as Nvidia's interim CEO.
articles.fullContent: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella weighed in on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unexpected departure amid a series of shocking controversies. “It’s all sort of pretty tragic in the sense of, you know, Jensen is somebody I’ve known for a long time. I’ve admired what he’s done, and at this point, I kind of want to give him space to figure this out,” Nadella said onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. Huang stepped down last week from his CEO role, which he has held for 33 years. Huang’s leadership has been central to Nvidia’s ascent to one of the world’s most valuable companies, but his judgment was questioned after it was reported that he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy feeding information back to Beijing. It was also revealed that Huang was having affairs with two Nvidia employees, including one who was a direct report. While the world waits to see what the long-term economic impacts of Huang’s departure might be, Nadella says he still has confidence in Nvidia, which is a close partner of Microsoft. “I’ll just say this one thing,” Nadella added. “Colette [Kress, interim CEO at Nvidia] worked at Microsoft for a long time. I’ve known her for a long time. She’s a tremendous person… I’m in touch with the same set of people I was in touch with before [Huang left], so I have a lot of confidence in the Nvidia team and their ability to continue to do the good work.” Microsoft is not unlike Nvidia in that its founder Bill Gates inhabited a larger-than-life persona as CEO. “Founders are unbelievable in the sense that they create something from nothing, so that is pretty magical… They’re singular, but they’re not gods, right?” Nadella said. “I used to say to Bill [Gates]… Founders also die, and so at some point, a company, if it needs to succeed, it has to have someone take over.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.title: Satya Nadella predicts AI agents will reshuffle the economics of the web
articles.contentSnippet: Microsoft's CEO says AI agents could disrupt advertising-driven business models, forcing companies like Amazon to rethink how they compete for customers.
articles.fullContent: In Brief Posted: 2:58 PM PST · November 18, 2026 Image Credits:Spencer Platt (opens in a new window) / Getty Images Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella predicts that the rise of AI agents is going to reshape the economics of the internet, impacting the business models of the companies that rely on advertising and what he referred to as “human web” traffic. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the tech executive argued that the shift to an agentic web could change which companies pay others for traffic and for transactions, similar to how the transition from web portals like Yahoo to search engines like Google did years ago. “The current aggregators who have a business model which was for the human web will get, in some sense, reshuffled,” said Nadella. “And if you were monetizing ads because of the eyeballs, you now have to probably get down to essentially maybe CPC [cost-per-click] wins; maybe it’s more transactional,” he continued. “And so if you don’t accept the agent, somebody else will.” The discussion turned to Amazon and its decision to block AI agents from accessing its retail website, preventing them from browsing its catalog and making purchases on behalf of their users. Nadella suggested that companies trying to protect their existing business models could lose out to others that are more willing to embrace the AI agents. For instance, if Amazon continues blocking agents, another shopping platform such as Shopify, could allow them, and gain an advantage. “I think this is going to be interesting,” he said, speaking to the changing models. “It’s the same thing that’s happening in other categories, right? Which is, if you’re in love with a particular business model, you have to kind of scramble,” he said. Newsletters Subscribe for the industry’s biggest tech news Related Latest in AI

articles.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 a share, above projected range
articles.contentSnippet: The long-awaited IPO reportedly values the company at $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis.
articles.fullContent: Anthropic has priced its long-awaited IPO at $83 per share, above its initial range of $70 to $78, signaling strong investor appetite for one of the companies at the center of the AI boom, despite market jitters following the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which shook confidence in the industry. The Claude maker sold 980 million shares in the offering, up from the 825 million initially planned, generating $81.3 billion in proceeds and surpassing SpaceX’s $75 billion record to become the largest IPO in history by proceeds raised. At the IPO price, Anthropic is valued at roughly $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, a significant increase from the $965 billion the company reached in May when it raised $65 billion in its last private market round, but below the $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for several months ago. Anthropic will begin its life as a public company on Thursday, trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” A strong first day of trading would signal that investors remain optimistic about AI adoption, despite recent volatility in AI-driven stocks. The company’s performance is expected to set expectations for private AI companies, including Anthropic’s main rival OpenAI, which was last reportedly valued at $1.25 billion but has yet to announce plans for an IPO. Although none of Anthropic’s venture capital investors holds more than a 5% stake in the company, the IPO is a massive windfall for its numerous backers. Investors who own approximately 1% of the company reportedly include Sequoia, as well as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC also holds about a 1% stake in the company, according to a person familiar with the matter. Other backers set to make billions are Iconiq, Menlo Ventures, Coatue, and Sound Ventures, a firm launched by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher. Spark Capital, the only VC firm known to hold a board seat at the company (it was the first institutional investor in the company, leading its $450 million Series C round in 2023 that valued the company at $4.5 billion), also stands to make a fortune off its early investment in Anthropic. Some of the Anthropic’s existing investors, namely Sequoia, Iconiq, Lightspeed, Accel, and Altimeter Capital Management, are so enthusiastic about Anthropic’s future that they are reportedly planning to buy billions of dollars’ worth of the company’s shares in the IPO. Yet the investors’ holdings in Anthropic pale in comparison to those of the company’s strategic partners Amazon, which owns nearly 15% of the company, and Google, which holds almost 14%. A group of major tech companies, including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners, have also agreed to purchase $26 billion worth of non-voting shares through a private placement alongside the IPO. The company’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, each sold nearly 3.4 million shares in the IPO, according to the S-1 filing, bringing in about $282 million for each. articles.title: Palmer Luckey doesn’t deny that he’s a prepper
articles.contentSnippet: The Anduril founder said Wednesday that Americans should always have three days of food, water, and medicine — just in case.
articles.fullContent: Defense mogul Palmer Luckey — whose $90 billion drone and weapons startup Anduril is flush with government contracts — is still the kind of guy who prepares for the worst. During Luckey’s conversation with Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the billionaire implied that Americans should batten down the hatches in case there are rough times ahead. Luckey himself has taken steps to prepare for a potential cataclysmic event, he said. The conversation took place against the backdrop of a series of recent large-scale outages — at Apple, at Microsoft, at the NSA, and at the Federal Aviation Administration — that have led to concerns that America may be under attack by cyberthreat actors. The government has said that this is not the case, but Luckey cryptically teased that there may be more to the story. “Look, all the 4chan schizo posters are like 12 hours ahead of the mainstream media on this. You guys are going to find out what’s going on soon enough,” he said. Sorkin also asked Luckey to expound on comments made backstage “about what might be a cyber war that seems to be going on around us.” Luckey described a “mismatch” between the sophisticated AI-powered cyberattacks that exist today and “old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed.” He added: “I think people are going to have to pick up the pace. It’s time to start running.” “What does that mean? Are you a prepper?” Sorkin asked. Luckey didn’t deny the characterization. “I own a missile base 200 feet underground,” he answered, to audience laughter. “It’s a funny joke, but a missile base is actually a pretty bad way to run from the apocalypse. Everyone knows exactly where you are, and they [bases] are designed to take a hit from a nuclear weapon, a blast overpressure event.” However, he had some qualifications on the prepper label. “The point is, like everyone should have three days of water. Everyone should have three days of dry food. If you have prescription medication, don’t go refill it when you run out. Make sure you refill it 72 hours before you run out.” “People used to be taught this in middle school, and now everyone who remembers that is treated like a nut,” he added. It should be pointed out that preparing for the apocalypse is not necessarily a new interest for Luckey. In 2017, a person familiar with the billionaire described him as a “prepper” and the bunker that was broached Wednesday is one of several decommissioned Cold War era underground bases that Luckey has purchased over the years. In 2024, he revealed that his massive video game collection is housed in one of them. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.title: Nvidia created a weird bit of intrigue by not filing a routine SEC report
articles.contentSnippet: One Wall Street analyst got to the bottom of Nvidia's surprise announcement that it wouldn't be filing its formal quarterly results document, the 10-Q, for weeks.
articles.fullContent: During Nvidia’s quarterly call on Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress dropped this little oddity: She said Nvidia wouldn’t be immediately filing its quarterly results report, known as a 10-Q, with the SEC. “We plan to file our 10-Q in the coming weeks.” And she offered no reason why. The delay was widely noticed. Among the many comments on X about it, economic and investment analyst Edward Dowd called it a “red flag.” Nvidia has typically filed the 10-Q the same day it reports results. The 10-Q offers far more detail about a company’s operations than an earnings press release, including sections that disclose “legal proceedings,” which include lawsuits that could affect the company; and “risk factors,” which cover other potentially business-impairing items. The announcement of the delay was so unusual that UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked about it after the public earnings call. Nvidia told him the delay was related to whether the company would need to disclose additional information about its ongoing investigation into Huang in the 10-Q. “The company announced that the 10-Q will be filed ‘in the coming weeks’ – later than usual. When queried on our callback, management indicated this was related to the ongoing investigation and whether any additional risk factors would need to be added to the filing,” Arcuri wrote in his research note. (Arcuri still rates the stock a “buy” by the way, although he did lower his price target to $220 from $240. The stock is now trading around $150). Notably, on the same day that Nvidia reported earnings, The Wall Street Journal reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors. So the mystery thickens: What will Nvidia disclose? We’ll have to wait and see. (Nvidia has not yet responded to our request for comment.) The delay suggests the company may have more to say about its mounting legal troubles. Nvidia is now facing multiple federal investigations over allegations that its partners were selling restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. So far, the scrutiny has come from a number of congressional committees; the Department of Justice looking into Megaspeed, the company run by a woman with whom Huang had an affair and who is also suspected of being a Chinese spy; and now, reportedly, the SEC. Additionally, Nvidia is conducting its own internal investigation into Huang after he admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang (the Megaspeed executive), and allegations surfaced that he also had affairs with other Nvidia employees. There’s little doubt that Wall Street will scrutinize that 10-Q once it’s finally filed. The intrigue brings to mind the old saying: “Doctors bury their mistakes. Lawyers put theirs in prison. And accountants hide theirs in the footnotes.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. articles.title: Palmer Luckey warns AI-powered cyberattacks are outpacing defenses: ‘It’s time to start running’
articles.contentSnippet: The Anduril co-founder says outdated technology is leaving systems vulnerable to a new wave of AI-enabled attacks.
articles.fullContent: AI-powered cyberattacks are moving faster than outdated technology systems can defend against them, Palmer Luckey warned at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. Addressing the recent spate of tech outages, the Oculus founder and Anduril Industries co-founder argued that older systems are struggling to keep pace with the new hacking capabilities enabled by AI and warned it was time to quicken the pace of securing our defenses. “We’re seeing the natural effects of a lot of these advanced AI tools allowing for the creation of various exploits,” he said. While government officials largely attributed the latest set of technical issues to companies rushing to patch their systems to protect against the new vulnerabilities AI has discovered, Luckey focused on the underlying security challenges facing organizations using outdated technology. Luckey explained that U.S. adversaries are currently exploiting the mismatch between new attack capabilities and our defense capabilities. These attacks are being carried out for both strategic and financial reasons, and North Korea was particularly involved, he added. The interviewer, Andrew Ross Sorkin, noted that U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance had canceled his appearance at the Times’ conference this week because of the recent tech outages, saying he now had to attend meetings about the matter. Given the situation, Sorkin asked Luckey how worried we should be about all this. “It depends on how well prepared you are,” was Luckey’s answer. (He then ominously warned, “You guys are going to find out what’s going on soon enough.”) The tech executive argued that AI could ultimately give defenders the upper hand, but they’d have to move more quickly. “In the long run, the advantages are going to accrue to the side that is most effectively using AI for defense,” Luckey said. “With the people who say that everything can be hacked — they are right, for now. That actually may be the case with certain new techniques that are coming along. But as of right now, there’s a mismatch between the attackers who are very fast-moving and using technology and old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed,” Luckey continued. “And I think … people are going to have to pick up the pace,” he said. “It’s time to start running.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.title: Palmer Luckey thinks China is ‘thrilled to have Jensen out,’ so he wants the ousted Nvidia CEO reinstated
articles.contentSnippet: "It makes America weaker to knock him out," the Anduril CEO said about ousted Nvidia leader Jensen Huang.

FALLON/AFP / Getty Images 1:31 PM PST · November 18, 2026 Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey thinks Nvidia’s board is giving China exactly what it wants by removing the company’s longtime CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang. Nvidia, the leading semiconductor designer whose chips power much of the AI industry, is undergoing a critical, unexpected leadership change. Huang, who led the company for 33 years, stepped down last week amid several controversies, including his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy who has been investigated for possibly smuggling Nvidia chips into China to circumvent U.S. export restrictions. “China wants Jensen out, so I want him in,” Luckey said onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, repeating a statement he posted on X last week. “They’re thrilled to have Jensen out… There’s a reason it’s knocking a trillion dollars off Nvidia’s market cap. They know it makes America weaker to knock him out.” Luckey disagrees with Huang’s longstanding position that Nvidia should have more leeway to export chips to China. But he also recognizes that China stands to benefit if its domestic chipmakers can challenge Nvidia’s dominance. “China doesn’t want Nvidia to sell GPUs to Chinese companies,” Luckey said. “There are Chinese companies that want to buy Nvidia GPUs… China will not give them an import permit because they want to build an internal domestic processor industry… not build one that is dependent on the United States.” Nvidia has said as much itself — the U.S. government granted the company license to ship some of its powerful H200 chips to certain Chinese customers, but those sales were restricted by the Chinese government. Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress said during the company’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday that it will no longer sell H200 chips in China at all. Luckey is far from alone among industry peers in his defense of Huang. More than 200,000 people — including Elon Musk and the CEOs of Y Combinator, Databricks, Epic Games, Shopify, and Replit — have signed a petition calling for Nvidia to reinstate its founder. But Nvidia executives said during the company’s earnings call on Tuesday that the company does not have plans to reappoint Huang, even though the founder offered to return. articles.title: Sam Altman says his life is so weird that he’s unfazed by Andrew Garfield portraying him in upcoming movie
articles.contentSnippet: "It doesn't feel like it's in like the top 10 weirdest things about my life," Altman said.
articles.fullContent: Hollywood has found plenty of material and cinematic inspiration from a string of Silicon Valley scandals and power struggles in recent years. “You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, smashed box office expectations, and Netflix’s limited series “The Altruists” comes out Thursday to tell the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the downfall of FTX. As the founder and CEO of OpenAI, one of the most influential companies of the century, Sam Altman isn’t going to escape the Hollywood treatment, either. In “Artificial,” a biographical comedy-drama opening in theaters on Christmas, the lauded actor Andrew Garfield will portray Altman in a film that chronicles OpenAI’s rise and the internal turmoil that erupted when he was briefly ousted in 2023. “If you had told me 20 years ago that someone was going to make a movie about me, I think that would have struck me as … that would have been a very weird thing,” Altman said onstage at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. “Now it doesn’t feel like it’s in like the top 10 weirdest things about my life.” Garfield is best known for his role as Spider-Man, but his big break came in 2010, when he played Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in “The Social Network” alongside Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg. (That film also had a sequel of sorts this year called “The Social Reckoning,” but it bombed at the box office.) So, if Altman isn’t fazed by the looming release of “Artificial,” what’s actually the weirdest thing in his life? “The fact that we are ushering in this technology that we have all of these very real concerns about, and that we have, we find ourselves in a role of such significance and such responsibility to make that go well,” Altman said. “That’s a crazy situation to find yourself in.” Sure, that is pretty weird, Sam. It’s also weird that you use ChatGPT for parenting advice and don’t respect olive oil. But I’d wager to say it’s even weirder that there’s an upcoming film about the time your colleagues briefly ousted you because they were concerned that you can’t be trusted. Say what you want about Mark Zuckerberg (I certainly have), but at least he’s honest about what he thinks about “The Social Network.” “It was weird, man,” Zuckerberg reflected on a podcast last year. “They got all these very specific details of what I was wearing, or these specific things correct, but then the whole narrative arc around my motivations and all this stuff were like, completely wrong … The whole arc is like, I’m somehow motivated by trying to find a girlfriend, [but] I was dating Priscilla [Chan] before I started Facebook.” Zuckerberg said he knew his employees would be tempted to see the movie, so he organized a company outing when it was released, even though the film hardly paints a flattering portrait of him. Zuckerberg even had enough of a sense of humor to buy a prop from the film at auction. He owns an Ardsley High School T-shirt that Eisenberg wore in the movie and even wore it himself in a video with YouTubers Colin and Samir. Eisenberg hasn’t been particularly complimentary of Zuckerberg, saying that he doesn’t want to think of himself as “associated with somebody like that.” And while “Artificial” hasn’t hit theaters yet, Garfield doesn’t seem to have a much more favorable opinion of the tech founder he portrays. “I don’t know Sam Altman. I’ve never met him,” Garfield told Esquire. “But I think anyone who takes on that level of responsibility for a company or technology that you know is going to do a hell of a lot of damage to the soul of humanity [must have] a certain ability to dissociate.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.title: Snapchat now lets developers build AR Lenses with AI assistants like Claude Code and Cursor
articles.contentSnippet: Lens creators can describe the Lens they want in plain language, and their AI assistant handles the process from start to finish, Snapchat says.
articles.fullContent: Snapchat announced on Wednesday that it’s giving Lens creators the ability to build Lenses using the AI coding assistants they already use, like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Snapchat Lenses, which are a core part of the social network’s platform, are AR effects that let users alter their appearance, add digital objects to their surroundings, or interact with animated experiences through the camera. The company is introducing Easy Lens CLI, which builds on its existing Easy Lens tool, which lets creators generate Lenses from a single prompt on the web and mobile. Easy Lens CLI brings that same idea into developers’ existing workflows, allowing AI assistants to handle the technical work while creators focus on the vision for the Lens itself. The launch indicates that Snapchat is looking to lower the barrier to creating AR content, while making its platform more accessible to developers who are increasingly using AI coding assistants. Instead of requiring creators to learn how to use Snapchat’s own development tools, the company is bringing Lens creation into the AI coding workflows they already use, which could in turn expand the pool of people who build for Snapchat. Image Credits:Snapchat Developers enrolled in Snapchat’s Lens+ Payouts program can earn from the Lenses they create with Easy Lens CLI. Snapchat says it paid out $1.8 million to Lens+ community creators last month. Lens creators can describe the Lens they want in plain language, and their AI assistant handles the process from start to finish, Snapchat says. That includes building with more than 100 AR building blocks and 50 AI asset generators, generating previews, and publishing them to Snapchat and tracking their performance. With Easy Lens CLI, Snapchat says developers can create everything from Web Lens games with leaderboards to camera effects and beauty filters. AI assistants can generate assets, build and test Lenses, address errors, and send updated versions directly to the creator’s phone. The new capability can take a game from an initial idea to a published Lens in a single day, without developers having to write code themselves, Snapchat says. The tool is aimed at different types of creators. The company notes that game developers can bring existing browser games to Snapchat as Web Lenses, while AI creators can use assets from their preferred tools to build Lenses in their own style. Additionally, agencies and brands can turn existing campaign videos, images, and other brand assets into AR experiences with less production time. Easy Lens CLI runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.
