articles.fullContent: Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0: BF16 FP8 NVFP4 The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings. Run DaisyRose-27B We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats. After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client: from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url="http://localhost:30000/v1", api_key="none", ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="DaisyRose-27B", messages=[ { "role": "user", "content": "How many positive divisors does 360 have?", } ], temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, extra_body={"top_k": 20, "min_p": 0.0}, ) print(response.choices[0].message.reasoning_content) print(response.choices[0].message.content) The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart. Benchmark results Benchmark Qwen3.8-27B DaisyRose-27B Terminal Bench 4.1 5.6 12.0 Terminal Bench 2.1 73.0 75.5 DeepSWE v1.1 42.2 46.2 SWE Bench Pro v2 91.3 94.7 HLE (text-only) 33.9 34.3 IFBench 79.5 82.4 GPQA Diamond 89.2 90.7 DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%. Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings. Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes. High-quality training data We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set. We selected tasks using three criteria: Each task targets a mistake the original model makes. We ran Qwen3.8-27B on every task and redesigned each one around the mistakes we wanted the model to stop making. We then adjusted the difficulty until the solve rate fell within a useful learning range. Each task requires several interdependent steps. The agent has to reason, plan, and execute across a long job. Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in a sandbox, with more than 100 tool calls and more than 256K output tokens. Tasks must reward actually solving the problem. We reviewed every task alongside the model’s attempts. Tasks that could be passed without solving the intended problem, or that contained a design flaw, were fixed or removed. Efficient training backend RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. articles.title: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say
articles.fullContent: Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs. A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon. GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move. Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon. We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors. The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs. The estimate everyone uses is compute-only For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time: T_theoretical = (6 · P · D) / (N_GPU · FLOPS_peak · MFU) Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance. This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O. These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart. To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range. What we built We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded. Two design choices shaped the work: Everything is known before dispatch. Every input comes from the submitted configuration: hyperparameters, dataset sizes, model identifiers, GPU allocation. No runtime logs, no partial progress. That is what makes the prediction usable for scheduling. Features that expose the overheads. articles.title: Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases
articles.fullContent: Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs. Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next. The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome. IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action. Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic. Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs. The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made. See how time series and real-time context come together to create value: Streamhouse: real-time data and intelligence for agentic era Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening. A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state. Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere. Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate. Figure 3. articles.fullContent: Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats. I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it. Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot. Add the plugin to Datasette (datasette install datasette-arrows) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option: This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release.

This is a helpful guide to the current leading models and sizes: Because of how distillation, RL, and benchmarking works, Neon technically outperforms Carbon by some measures despite being a smaller model… Also today, Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, above its initial range, and Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy Applied Compute in a $4.5B all-stock deal. Neon is coming to the paid Gemini API in AI Studio and Android Studio, Gemini for business, and Antigravity for Pro and Ultra subscribers. In the Gemini app, Pro and Ultra users can select it as “Deeper analysis,” including for Tasks. Google’s rollout · Gemini appDay-one integrations. Neon debuted second with 1,336 points across about 4,200 sessions. It had a $2.82 median task cost and placed second on steerability. Carbon still leads the separate Text Arena. Agent Arena · Text ArenaVals. Neon placed second on the Vals Index at 70.9%, about 0.4 points behind Fable 5.2 at less than half the cost per task. On Code Migration it averaged 160 turns, fewer than Carbon’s 234 or Hydrogen’s 574, and scored below both. Vals Index · Code MigrationCursorBench 4.1. The logs also recorded 57 capacity errors and four stalled runs. Test logsHow teams use it. Theo says he’s now using Neon for copy, Fable to implement changes, and Astra to playtest.
